stemBlocks.value: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, ∠PQR = 120° and QR = 5 cm.
Think first: This is a side–angle–side construction, and 120° is simply 180° minus a constructed 60°.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p159-q16 from workbook page 159.

solutionSteps.instruction: Extend PQ beyond Q to give a straight line through Q.

contentBlocks.value: 120° is the supplement of 60°, so a 60° angle measured from the extension gives 120° with QP

solutionSteps.instruction: Construct 60° at Q from the extension.

contentBlocks.value: Centre Q, arc cutting the line; same radius from that intersection cuts the arc — join Q to the crossing

solutionSteps.instruction: Mark R on that arm with QR = 5 cm.

contentBlocks.value: Compasses set to 5 cm, centre Q

solutionSteps.instruction: Join PR and check its length.

strategyBlocks.value: Draw PQ = 8 cm, construct 120° at Q by building 60° from the extension of PQ, mark R 5 cm along that arm, and join PR.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: A correctly constructed triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, QR = 5 cm and the included angle ∠PQR = 120°. Accuracy check: PR ≈ 11.4 cm.

whyThisWorks.value: Two sides and the angle between them fix a triangle uniquely, which is why side–angle–side works as a construction. Because 60° is the one angle compasses give directly (from an equilateral triangle), every multiple and supplement of 60° — 30°, 90°, 120° — is reachable by combining that construction with bisection or extension.

commonErrors.misconception: Drawing the 60° on the wrong side of Q, producing 60° instead of 120°.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Drawing the 60° on the wrong side of Q, producing 60° instead of 120°.

commonErrors.misconception: Marking QR = 5 cm along QP instead of along the new arm.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Marking QR = 5 cm along QP instead of along the new arm.

commonErrors.misconception: Checking with Pythagoras — the triangle is obtuse, not right-angled, so the cosine rule is the correct check.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Checking with Pythagoras — the triangle is obtuse, not right-angled, so the cosine rule is the correct check.

examTip.value: Remember the compass angle family: 60° direct, 30° by bisecting it, 90° by perpendicular, 120° as 180° − 60°. Recognising which one a question wants saves minutes.
